exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Dimension of a Span by Inspection

question.explanation:
We start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to basis vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the reduced matrix has $3$ pivot columns (or alternatively, $3$ non-zero rows).

Therefore, the dimension of the span is $3.$

example.title: Finding the Dimension of a Span by Inspection

question.text:
Let $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3$ be linearly independent vectors, and suppose that the vector $\mathbf{w}$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3$ form a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\}$
  2. $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\} \big) = 4$
  3. $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{w} \big\} \big) = 3$
question.explanation:
Recall that a basis of a vector space $V$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that span $V.$ The dimension of $V$ is the number of vectors in any basis of $V$ (if such a basis exists).

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\}$ is spanned by $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3$, and we are told that $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3$ are linearly independent vectors. So, $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3$ is a basis of the span.

  • Statement II is false. Since $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3$ is a basis of the given span and this basis contains $3$ vectors, we have $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\} \big) = 3$ (not $4$).

  • Statement III is false. We are told that $\mathbf{w}$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2.$ This means that $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{w} \big\}$ is completely spanned by the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2$ only. So, $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{w} \big\} \big) = 2$ (not $3$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

example.title: Finding the Dimension of a Span by Inspection

question.text:
Let $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$ be linearly independent vectors, and suppose that the vector $\mathbf{w}$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3+\mathbf{v}_4.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$ form a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4\big\}$
  2. $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4 \big\} \big) = 4$
  3. $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4, \mathbf{w} \big\} \big) = 5$
question.explanation:
Recall that a basis of a vector space $V$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that span $V.$ The dimension of $V$ is the number of vectors in any basis of $V$ (if such a basis exists).

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4\big\}$ is spanned by the vectors by $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4.$ Moreover, $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$ are linearly independent vectors. So, $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$ is a basis of the span.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4 \big\}$ is spanned by $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$, and these are linearly independent vectors. So, $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$ is a basis of the span. Therefore, we have $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4 \big\} \big) = 4.$

  • Statement III is false. We are told that $\mathbf{w}$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3+\mathbf{v}_4.$ Hence,$\mathbf{w}$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4.$ this means that $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4, \mathbf{w} \big\}$ is completely spanned by $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4$ only. So, $\text{dim}\big( \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3,\mathbf{v}_4,\mathbf{w} \big\} \big) = 4$ (not $5$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Dimension of a Span Using Row Reduction

question.explanation:
We start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

\begin{align*} \phantom{M} &\phantom{=\:\,} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & 12 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2+(-2)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & 12 \end{bmatrix} & R_3 &:= R_3+(-1)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & 12 \end{bmatrix} & R_4 &:= R_4+(-4)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

The pivot columns correspond to basis vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the reduced matrix has $3$ pivot columns (or alternatively, it has exactly $3$ non-zero rows).

Therefore, $ \textrm{dim} \left( \textrm{Span} \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix} \right\} \right) = 3. $
